title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
hook: Vishnu offers Shiva a lotus for every name, and at the last name, the lotus is gone

segments.voice: Last time the Shiva Sahasranama gave us Pashupati, lord of every creature, the one who loosens the rope. Which rope did you give an inch of slack? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.
screen: `PASHUPATI LOOSENS THE ROPE.` · `A NEW WEEK, A NEW STORY.`

segments.voice: One lotus is missing. Vishnu has been at this for a long time, kneeling before Shiva, saying a name and laying down a lotus, a name and a lotus, over and over. There should be a flower for every name. And now, with one name left to say, his hand reaches into the basket and finds nothing. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it, and it's how that Purana frames its own list of Shiva's names. Today's selection from the Shiva Sahasranama is a story about the hymn itself.
screen: `A NAME, A LOTUS.` → `ONE NAME LEFT.` → `THE BASKET IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana, Vishnu needs Shiva's help. The demons are winning, and Vishnu goes to Shiva's shrine to worship him. He sets out to honor him with a thousand names, offering a lotus at each one. Shiva decides to test him, and quietly hides one lotus. So we're back at the empty basket. What does Vishnu do? He could stop and say the worship is done well enough. He could leave and come back with more flowers. Instead he remembers what people call him: Kamala-nayana, the lotus-eyed. His eyes are lotuses, he thinks. So he means to offer one of them. And as he reaches to take out his own eye, Shiva appears and stops him, delighted. Shiva gives him a gift: the Sudarshana, the blazing discus Vishnu carries in his hand from then on. The story does a few things at once. It makes the hymn of Shiva's names part of the story of how Vishnu received his discus. It shows two great gods, often worshipped by different communities, held together in a single scene of devotion, with no one shamed. And it says something about what the names are for. Vishnu wasn't reciting a list to get to the end of it. Every name was a real offering, and when the offering ran short, he gave what he had. The last name mattered as much as the first. On an ordinary day, that's the hard part of any long practice: the last name, the last rep, the last page, said like it still counts.
screen: `VISHNU: A NAME AND A LOTUS EACH.` · `SHIVA HIDES ONE LOTUS.` · `THE LOTUS-EYED OFFERS HIS EYE.` · `THE SUDARSHANA, A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat each breath as a lotus. Sit, and let the breath find its pace. On each in-breath, gather something small to offer: a person you're grateful for, a moment from today, a plain thank you. On each out-breath, lay it down. A breath, an offering. The point isn't how many. It's whether the latest one is as real as the first. When your attention wanders, that's your empty basket: just come back, and give the next breath. If you pray, you can offer each breath to Shiva, or to God. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's selection: the Shiva Purana's story of Vishnu offering a lotus at every name, and his own eye when one went missing.
Your line: the Shiva Sahasranama, in selections. Today, at the end of something long, give the last piece the same care as the first. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Hindus tell this story of Vishnu's lotuses in the Shiva Purana, and in a Shiva temple a devotee may sponsor an archana in which a flower is offered at each of Shiva's names.

notes: Selection four of seven; first day of a new week (1135–1141). Paraphrased from the Shiva Purana, Koti Rudra Samhita: Vishnu, troubled by the demons, worships Shiva with a thousand names and a lotus at each; Shiva hides one; Vishnu, called lotus-eyed (kamala-nayana / padmaksha), resolves to offer his eye; Shiva stops him and gives the Sudarshana. 'A thousand names' is said because the text says it. Confirm details and chapter.
'It's how that Purana frames its own list of Shiva's names': the Shiva Purana's sahasranama is set in this episode as the names Vishnu recited. Confirm.

'Two great gods, often worshipped by different communities, held together ... with no one shamed': framing to avoid a Shaiva-versus-Vaishnava reading. Vaishnava texts tell the Sudarshana's origin differently; not mentioned. Keeper may want a line saying other texts tell it otherwise.
